items.text: “A 24-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal pain and vaginal discharge. Take a focused history.”
“Examine a patient with suspected PID and present your findings.”
“Discuss the investigations and management of a woman with pelvic inflammatory disease.”
“A woman with PID has severe pelvic pain and fever. How would you assess her for complications?”
“Counsel a patient newly diagnosed with PID about treatment, fertility and prevention of recurrence.”

blocks.text: Your immediate priorities are to assess the patient's stability, exclude pregnancy-related emergencies and other surgical causes, and determine whether outpatient treatment is appropriate.
Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract, potentially involving:

items.text: Endometrium — endometritis.
Fallopian tubes — salpingitis.
Ovaries and adjacent tissues — oophoritis or pelvic inflammation.
Pelvic peritoneum — pelvic peritonitis.
Formation of a collection involving the tube and ovary — tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA).

blocks.text: Infection commonly ascends from the cervix or vagina. Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are important sexually transmitted pathogens, but PID is often polymicrobial. Vaginal anaerobes and other organisms may contribute, and negative gonorrhoea or chlamydia tests do not exclude PID.

items.text: Previous PID.
Previous or current sexually transmitted infection.
A new sexual partner or multiple partners.
A partner with other sexual partners or a known STI.
Inconsistent condom use.
Previous STI exposure or untreated infection.
Recent uterine instrumentation or pregnancy-related procedures in relevant circumstances.
Younger age is associated with increased STI risk in many populations, but PID can occur at any reproductive age.

blocks.text: Avoid stigmatising assumptions: PID is a clinical diagnosis, not a judgement about a patient's behaviour.
Typical symptoms

items.text: Bilateral lower abdominal or pelvic pain.
Abnormal vaginal discharge.
Deep dyspareunia.
Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Painful menstruation.
Fever, nausea or malaise in more severe disease.

blocks.text: Examination findings

items.text: Lower abdominal tenderness.
Cervical motion tenderness.
Uterine tenderness.
Adnexal tenderness.
Mucopurulent cervical discharge or cervical friability.
Fever or systemic illness in some patients.

blocks.text: PID may be mild or asymptomatic. A patient does not need to have fever, purulent discharge or all three classic tenderness findings for PID to be present.

“Good morning. My name is …, and I am one of the doctors looking after you. I understand that you have been experiencing lower abdominal pain. I would like to ask about your symptoms, menstrual and sexual health, and any previous infections to help determine the cause. Some questions are personal, but your answers will be treated confidentially. Is that okay?”

items.text: Confirm the patient's identity.
Ensure privacy and confidentiality.
Use neutral, non-judgemental language.
Ask permission before taking a sexual history.
Explain and obtain consent before an intimate examination.
Offer a chaperone according to local policy.

rows: S — Site
“Where is the pain? Is it on one side or both?”
Bilateral pelvic pain may occur in PID; unilateral pain raises concern for other causes, including torsion or ectopic pregnancy.
O — Onset
“When did it start? Was it sudden or gradual?”
Gradual pain with discharge may suggest infection; sudden severe pain requires urgent assessment.
C — Character
“Is it sharp, cramping, aching or constant?”
Helps characterise severity and possible alternative diagnoses.
R — Radiation
“Does it spread to your back, groin or rectum?”
May help identify associated urinary, gastrointestinal or pelvic pathology.
A — Associated symptoms
“Have you noticed discharge, fever, bleeding, painful urination or vomiting?”
Helps assess PID and complications, while identifying alternative diagnoses.
T — Timing
“Is it constant or intermittent? Is it related to your period or intercourse?”
Helps identify cyclical disease and symptom progression.
E — Exacerbating/relieving factors
“Does movement, intercourse or urination make it worse?”
Movement-related pain or peritoneal signs may suggest more severe pathology.
S — Severity
“On a scale of 0–10, how severe is it?”
Helps determine urgency, analgesia needs and possible admission.

items.text: When did the discharge begin?
Has its quantity, colour or smell changed?
Is it associated with itching or irritation?
Is there bleeding between periods or after intercourse?
Is menstruation unusually heavy or painful?
Is there bleeding after a recent procedure or pregnancy-related event?

blocks.text: Interpretation: mucopurulent discharge with pelvic pain supports the possibility of cervicitis or PID, but discharge alone does not establish the diagnosis.

content_groups.group_title: D. Menstrual, obstetric and pregnancy history

items.text: First day of the last menstrual period.
Usual cycle regularity and menstrual pattern.
Possibility of pregnancy and contraceptive use.
Previous pregnancies, miscarriages, ectopic pregnancy or termination of pregnancy.
Recent delivery, miscarriage, abortion or uterine instrumentation, if relevant.
Future fertility wishes.

blocks.text: Always consider ectopic pregnancy in a patient with pelvic pain and possible pregnancy. Do not assume that contraception completely excludes pregnancy.

items.text: Are you currently sexually active?
Do you have a new sexual partner?
Have you or your partner been diagnosed with an STI?
Have you had an STI or PID before?
Have you been tested or treated recently?
Do you use condoms?
Is there any possibility that a partner has not been treated for an infection?

blocks.text: Explain why you are asking:
“These questions help us identify infections that may require treatment for both you and your partner, and they help reduce the chance of the infection returning.”
Do not assume that a positive STI test establishes when or from whom an infection was acquired.

content_groups.group_title: F. Previous treatment and medical history

items.text: Previous episodes of PID or cervicitis.
Recent antibiotics and whether a full course was completed.
Drug allergies, especially antibiotic allergies.
Previous pelvic or abdominal surgery.
Known endometriosis, fibroids, ovarian cysts or fertility problems.
Relevant medical conditions, including immunosuppression.
Current medications and possible interactions.

content_groups.group_title: G. Screen for complications and emergencies

items.text: Severe or worsening pain.
Fever, rigors or persistent vomiting.
Fainting, dizziness or shoulder-tip pain.
Heavy vaginal bleeding.
Abdominal distension.
Inability to tolerate oral fluids or medication.
Pregnancy possibility.
Symptoms suggesting sepsis.

blocks.text: These findings may indicate ectopic pregnancy, tubo-ovarian abscess, peritonitis or another acute abdominal emergency.

content_groups.group_title: A. Initial assessment: ABCDE when indicated

blocks.text: If the patient is acutely unwell, begin with an ABCDE assessment and summon senior assistance as needed.

items.text: A — Airway: assess patency.
B — Breathing: respiratory rate and oxygen saturation.
C — Circulation: pulse, blood pressure, capillary refill, perfusion and signs of bleeding or dehydration.
D — Disability: mental status and consciousness.
E — Exposure: temperature, abdominal findings, discharge or bleeding, maintaining dignity.

blocks.text: Obtain intravenous access, blood samples and fluid resuscitation when clinically indicated. Escalate promptly if there is shock, sepsis or suspected surgical pathology.

items.text: Temperature.
Pulse and blood pressure.
Respiratory rate and oxygen saturation.
General appearance and hydration.
Pallor or signs of significant bleeding.
Features of systemic infection.

blocks.text: Normal report:
“The patient is alert, comfortable at rest, afebrile and haemodynamically stable, with no obvious signs of systemic illness.”
Abnormal report:

“The patient is febrile and tachycardic, with lower abdominal pain and clinical signs of dehydration. I would assess for severe PID, tubo-ovarian abscess and sepsis, and arrange urgent senior review.”
Inspect, palpate, percuss and auscultate as appropriate.

items.text: Lower abdominal tenderness.
Suprapubic or iliac fossa tenderness.
Guarding or rebound tenderness.
Abdominal distension.
A palpable mass.
Signs of peritonism.
“There is bilateral lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound tenderness.”
“There is marked lower abdominal tenderness with involuntary guarding, raising concern for peritoneal irritation.”
“There is a palpable lower abdominal mass associated with tenderness; a tubo-ovarian abscess or other pelvic mass must be considered.”

blocks.text: With consent and a chaperone, inspect the vagina and cervix.

items.text: Vaginal discharge.
Mucopurulent cervical discharge.
Cervical erythema or friability.
Contact bleeding.
Visible lesions or retained foreign material where relevant.

blocks.text: Example report:

“Speculum examination reveals mucopurulent endocervical discharge and cervical friability. Samples are obtained for appropriate STI testing. These findings support cervicitis and increase suspicion of PID in the presence of pelvic pain.”

items.text: Cervical motion tenderness.
Uterine tenderness.
Adnexal tenderness.
Adnexal or pelvic mass.

blocks.text: Example report:

“Bimanual examination demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness. In the context of lower abdominal pain and abnormal discharge, these findings support a clinical diagnosis of PID.”
Remember that cervical motion tenderness is not specific to PID. It may also occur in ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis and other pelvic or abdominal conditions.
If the patient has severe pain or an examination would be intolerable, do not force the examination; prioritise safety, consent and appropriate investigations.
The aim is to support the diagnosis, identify the causative organism, assess severity, exclude emergencies and detect complications.

rows: Urine or serum β-hCG
Exclude pregnancy-related complications, particularly ectopic pregnancy
Vaginal or endocervical swabs / appropriate NAAT
Test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; test for other infections according to clinical context
Full blood count
Assess leukocytosis and anaemia where relevant
CRP or ESR
Assess inflammation; normal results do not exclude PID
Urinalysis and urine culture
Investigate urinary infection or other urinary causes of pain
HIV and syphilis testing
Screen for other STIs, with informed consent and appropriate counselling
Pelvic ultrasound
Assess for tubo-ovarian abscess, adnexal pathology, free fluid and alternative diagnoses

blocks.text: A positive STI test supports the diagnosis, but negative cervical tests do not rule out upper genital tract infection. Do not delay appropriate empiric treatment while awaiting results when clinical suspicion is sufficient.
STI Treatment Guidelines

content_groups.group_title: B. When is imaging particularly important?

blocks.title: Request pelvic ultrasound promptly when there is:

items.text: Severe or unilateral pain.
A palpable pelvic mass.
Suspected tubo-ovarian abscess.
Pregnancy or possible ectopic pregnancy.
Diagnostic uncertainty.
Failure to improve with treatment.

blocks.text: CT or MRI may be needed in selected cases when the diagnosis remains uncertain or other abdominal and pelvic pathology must be evaluated.
Scenario 1 — uncomplicated PID is likely
Pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness and mucopurulent discharge, without a palpable mass or systemic instability.
Interpretation: treat clinically suspected PID while testing for STIs and evaluating alternative diagnoses.
Scenario 2 — possible tubo-ovarian abscess
Fever, marked pelvic tenderness, systemic illness and a complex adnexal mass on ultrasound.
Interpretation: urgent gynaecological assessment, hospital admission and parenteral antibiotics; drainage or surgery may be required.
Scenario 3 — positive chlamydia NAAT
Pelvic pain and cervical motion tenderness with a positive chlamydia test.
Interpretation: chlamydia is identified, but upper genital tract infection may involve additional organisms. Treat PID with a recommended broad-spectrum regimen rather than chlamydia treatment alone.
Scenario 4 — negative STI tests but persistent pelvic tenderness
PID remains clinically plausible, but alternative diagnoses must also be considered.
Interpretation: reassess the diagnosis, severity, prior antibiotic exposure and possible complications rather than excluding PID solely because STI tests are negative.

PID is often diagnosed clinically. In a sexually active patient or another patient at risk of STIs who has pelvic or lower abdominal pain, consider empiric treatment when no better explanation is identified and at least one of these examination findings is present:

items.text: Cervical motion tenderness.
Uterine tenderness.
Adnexal tenderness.

blocks.text: Additional findings, such as fever, mucopurulent discharge, inflammatory markers or positive STI tests, increase diagnostic confidence. These criteria are intentionally sensitive because delayed treatment can lead to reproductive complications.
STI Treatment Guidelines

rows: Ectopic pregnancy
Positive pregnancy test, unilateral pain, vaginal bleeding, dizziness or syncope
Ovarian torsion
Sudden severe unilateral pain, often with nausea or vomiting
Appendicitis
Right iliac fossa pain, anorexia, nausea and possible peritoneal signs
Ruptured or haemorrhagic ovarian cyst
Sudden pelvic pain, sometimes with internal bleeding
UTI or pyelonephritis
Urinary symptoms, flank pain or fever
Endometriosis
Recurrent cyclical pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia or infertility
Gastroenteritis or bowel pathology
Gastrointestinal symptoms and bowel-related pain

blocks.text: Examiner's point: never anchor on PID when ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, appendicitis or another surgical emergency has not been adequately considered.
Management depends on severity, pregnancy status, ability to take oral medication, likelihood of complications and response to treatment.

items.text: Assess vital signs and overall stability.
Provide appropriate analgesia and antiemetics if required.
Perform a pregnancy test and investigate important alternative diagnoses.
Obtain appropriate STI samples and other investigations.
Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly when indicated.
Decide whether outpatient care is safe or hospital admission is required.
Explain treatment, partner management, sexual precautions and follow-up.

blocks.text: For mild to moderate acute PID in a non-pregnant patient who is clinically stable and can tolerate oral medication, a commonly used CDC regimen is:

rows: Ceftriaxone
500 mg intramuscularly once
Doxycycline
100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
Metronidazole
500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days

blocks.text: These medicines are used together as a regimen, not as interchangeable alternatives. This example follows CDC guidance; the appropriate local protocol, antimicrobial resistance patterns, allergy history, pregnancy status and patient-specific contraindications must be checked before prescribing.
STI Treatment Guidelines

items.text: Complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve.
Discuss possible adverse effects and relevant medicine precautions.
Review allergies, drug interactions and pregnancy possibility before prescribing.
If the patient is pregnant or pregnancy cannot be adequately excluded, obtain appropriate senior or specialist guidance rather than automatically using the routine outpatient regimen.

content_groups.group_title: C. When should the patient be admitted?

blocks.text: **Admission criteria — remember S-T-A-B-L-E**

items.text: S — Severe illness, significant fever, vomiting or systemic toxicity.
T — Tubo-ovarian abscess suspected or confirmed.
A — Acute surgical emergency cannot be excluded.
B — Being pregnant.
L — Lack of response to outpatient treatment.
E — Eating or tolerating oral medication is not possible, or outpatient treatment is not feasible.

blocks.text: Hospital admission is also appropriate when pain is severe or uncontrolled, follow-up cannot be assured, or specialist assessment is needed.
STI Treatment Guidelines

blocks.title: For severe PID or suspected complications:

items.text: Admit and involve the gynaecology team promptly.
Provide appropriate IV fluids if indicated, analgesia and antiemetics.
Obtain cultures and other relevant tests without delaying treatment.
Start a recommended broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotic regimen according to the hospital protocol.
Monitor vital signs, urine output when indicated, pain and clinical response.
Investigate for tubo-ovarian abscess, ectopic pregnancy and other surgical pathology.
Transition to oral therapy when the patient has improved, completing the recommended total treatment course.

blocks.text: A commonly recommended CDC parenteral option is IV ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and metronidazole, with route and dosing determined by severity and clinical circumstances. Alternative regimens may be required for allergies, intolerance or other patient-specific factors.
STI Treatment Guidelines
A tubo-ovarian abscess is a potentially serious complication.

items.text: Hospital admission and urgent gynaecological review.
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
Monitoring for rupture, sepsis and clinical deterioration.
Consideration of image-guided drainage or surgery if the abscess is large, rupture is suspected, the patient deteriorates or adequate improvement does not occur.

blocks.text: The decision to drain or operate depends on the clinical state, imaging, response to antibiotics and specialist assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Partner management and sexual health counselling

blocks.text: This is an important OSCE marking area. Treating the patient alone may not prevent reinfection if a partner has an untreated STI.

items.text: Recent sexual partners should be assessed, tested and treated as indicated under local STI guidance.
Partner notification should be handled confidentially and without blame.
The patient should avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is completed, symptoms have resolved and relevant partners have been treated.
Offer testing for gonorrhoea, chlamydia, HIV and syphilis, as appropriate.
Discuss consistent condom use and repeat STI testing when recommended by the relevant guideline.
If the infection is associated with sexual exposure, explain that it does not by itself establish when or from whom the infection was acquired.

blocks.text: For PID associated with gonorrhoea or chlamydia, partner management is particularly important.
STI Treatment Guidelines
1. Tubal infertility
Inflammation can damage the fallopian tube lining and impair ovum transport. Recurrent episodes increase the risk of tubal damage.
2. Ectopic pregnancy
Tubal damage increases the risk that a future pregnancy implants outside the uterus, most commonly in the fallopian tube.
3. Tubo-ovarian abscess
Pus collects around the tube and ovary. Rupture can cause peritonitis and sepsis.
4. Chronic pelvic pain
Persistent inflammation and adhesions may contribute to long-term pain, dyspareunia and reduced quality of life.
Other complications include recurrent PID and, less commonly, severe systemic infection or inflammation involving adjacent abdominal structures.
Exam pearl: early, appropriate treatment reduces the risk of complications but cannot guarantee that established tubal damage will be reversed.
STI Treatment Guidelines
Review the patient within 48–72 hours after starting outpatient treatment.

items.text: Whether pain is improving.
Temperature and general condition.
Abdominal and pelvic tenderness.
Medication adherence and adverse effects.
STI test results and whether treatment needs adjustment.
Whether partner management has been addressed.

blocks.text: If there is no meaningful clinical improvement by 72 hours, the patient needs reassessment and often hospital admission. Reconsider the diagnosis, check for an abscess or alternative pathology, and review the antibiotic regimen.
STI Treatment Guidelines
Scenario: A 23-year-old woman has been diagnosed with PID and is worried about infertility.
Step 1 — Explain the diagnosis

“Your symptoms and examination suggest an infection involving the upper reproductive tract, which we call pelvic inflammatory disease. This can cause pelvic pain, discharge and sometimes abnormal bleeding.”
Step 2 — Reassure without making promises

“The good news is that early treatment is important and can reduce the risk of complications. Some women develop scarring of the fallopian tubes, which may affect fertility, but having PID does not automatically mean that you will be infertile.”
Step 3 — Explain treatment

“We recommend antibiotics that cover the likely organisms. It is important to take them as prescribed and complete the course. We will also check whether you need hospital treatment or additional investigations.”
Step 4 — Discuss partners sensitively

“Depending on the infection and your recent sexual history, your sexual partner or partners may need assessment and treatment. This helps prevent the infection returning. We can discuss confidential ways to arrange this.”
Step 5 — Discuss sexual activity
“Please avoid sexual intercourse until you have completed treatment, your symptoms have resolved and relevant partners have been treated.”
Step 6 — Safety-net and follow-up

“I would like to review you within two to three days to make sure you are improving. If you develop severe or worsening pain, fever, fainting, persistent vomiting or heavy bleeding, seek urgent medical care.”
Step 7 — Invite questions
“What worries you most about this diagnosis? Is there anything about the treatment, fertility or partner notification that you would like us to discuss?”

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the most important examination finding in suspected PID?

There is no single definitive finding. Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness or adnexal tenderness in a patient with pelvic pain and no better explanation can support a presumptive clinical diagnosis.
Q2. Must the patient have fever to have PID?
No. PID can be mild, atypical or asymptomatic. The absence of fever does not exclude it.
Q3. Does a negative chlamydia test exclude PID?
No. PID is frequently polymicrobial, and infection may involve organisms other than chlamydia. A negative cervical test does not exclude upper genital tract infection.
Q4. Why should treatment not be delayed unnecessarily?
Delayed treatment increases the risk of ongoing inflammation and reproductive complications, including tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
Q5. What are the indications for admission?
Pregnancy, suspected tubo-ovarian abscess, severe illness, inability to tolerate outpatient treatment, failure of outpatient treatment, or inability to exclude a surgical emergency.
Q6. What is a tubo-ovarian abscess?
A collection of pus involving the fallopian tube and ovary, usually as a complication of pelvic infection. It requires hospital treatment and may require drainage or surgery.
Q7. When should you review outpatient PID?
Within 48–72 hours. Failure to improve by 72 hours requires reassessment and escalation of care.
Q8. Why must sexual partners be managed?
To identify and treat relevant infections, prevent reinfection and reduce ongoing transmission.
Q9. What are the major long-term complications?
Tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain and recurrent PID. Tubo-ovarian abscess is an important acute complication.
Q10. What would you do if the patient has a positive pregnancy test and suspected PID?

Arrange urgent obstetric/gynaecological assessment, exclude ectopic pregnancy and other emergencies, and initiate specialist-directed treatment appropriate for pregnancy. The routine outpatient regimen should not automatically be used.

blocks.text: Remember to assess the patient's response within 48–72 hours. If she is not improving, reconsider the diagnosis, complications and need for admission.
1. A patient has pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness and no better alternative diagnosis. What is the best next step?
Wait for all STI results before treating
Consider presumptive PID treatment and investigate appropriately
Diagnose endometriosis immediately
Arrange hysterectomy
2. Which finding is an indication for hospital admission?
Mild pain with stable vital signs and good oral intake
A history of dysmenorrhoea alone
Suspected tubo-ovarian abscess
A normal pelvic ultrasound in an otherwise improving patient
3. A patient treated as an outpatient has not improved after 72 hours. What should you do?
Continue the same treatment indefinitely
Reassess the diagnosis, investigate complications and consider admission
Stop all antibiotics without reassessment
Assume the symptoms are psychological
4. Which statement about a negative chlamydia test is correct?
It excludes PID
It excludes all sexually transmitted infections
It does not exclude PID
It proves the infection has resolved
5. Which is a major long-term complication of PID?
Tubal infertility
Cervical ectropion in every patient
Universal ovarian failure
Endometrial cancer
